white-house.name: White House
white-house.clue: Painted sandstone walls give this house its name, and every president of its country has lived here since 1800. British troops set it on fire in 1814.
white-house.blurb: The Irish-born architect James Hoban won the design competition and modelled the house on Leinster House in Dublin, today home to the Irish parliament. Built between 1792 and 1800 from Aquia Creek sandstone painted white, it has housed every US president since John Adams. British troops set it on fire in 1814, during the War of 1812, and it had to be rebuilt. Thomas Jefferson added the low colonnades on each wing to hide the stables and storage. Its name is also shorthand for the presidency itself.

st-peter-s-basilica.name: St Peter's Basilica
st-peter-s-basilica.architect: Bramante, Michelangelo, Carlo Maderno and Gian Lorenzo Bernini
st-peter-s-basilica.clue: Michelangelo's dome crowns the largest church on Earth, at the heart of the world's smallest country, while a colonnade opens in front of it like two embracing arms.
st-peter-s-basilica.blurb: It replaced a fourth-century basilica built by Emperor Constantine, which had grown old and unsafe. Building began in 1506 and took 120 years, passing through the hands of Bramante, Raphael, Michelangelo and Carlo Maderno, who added the long nave and the front. Michelangelo designed the great dome but died before it was finished. Bernini later shaped the vast oval piazza, its colonnades meant to embrace visitors like the arms of the church. Tradition holds that Saint Peter is buried beneath the high altar.

palace-of-versailles.name: Palace of Versailles
palace-of-versailles.architect: Louis Le Vau, Jules Hardouin-Mansart and André Le Nôtre
palace-of-versailles.clue: A Hall of Mirrors in a palace built to glorify the Sun King, just outside a great capital. The royal court lived here until an angry crowd marched out from the city in 1789.
palace-of-versailles.blurb: Louis XIV turned his father's hunting lodge into the grandest palace in Europe, to glorify the monarchy and keep the nobles close where he could watch them. The king, the court and the government lived here from 1682 until October 1789, when a crowd marched from Paris and forced the royal family back to the capital. Le Vau, Hardouin-Mansart and the garden designer Le Nôtre created the ensemble, including the dazzling Hall of Mirrors. Courts all over Europe copied its style. Today it is a museum and one of the most visited sites in France.

cologne-cathedral.name: Cologne Cathedral
cologne-cathedral.architect: Master Gerhard; completed by Ernst Friedrich Zwirner
cologne-cathedral.clue: Twin lacy spires, the tallest of any cathedral, tower beside a busy railway station on the Rhine. Work stopped for nearly 300 years, with a medieval crane left standing on top.
cologne-cathedral.blurb: Building began in 1248 to house relics believed to be those of the Three Kings, but work stopped around 1560 with the church half finished. For centuries a medieval crane stood on the unfinished south tower as part of the skyline. Interest in Gothic revived in the 19th century, and the cathedral was completed to its original medieval plan in 1880. At 157 m its twin spires make it the tallest cathedral in the world. It is Germany's most visited landmark, with about 6 million visitors a year.

willis-tower.name: Willis Tower
willis-tower.architect: Bruce Graham and Fazlur Khan (Skidmore, Owings & Merrill)
willis-tower.clue: Black steel tubes bundled together, stepping back as they climb above a windy lakeside city. High up, glass boxes stick out from the wall so visitors can stand over thin air.
willis-tower.blurb: Still widely called the Sears Tower, it opened in 1973 as the tallest building in the world, a title it held for nearly 25 years. Architect Bruce Graham and engineer Fazlur Khan of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill bundled square steel tubes together and stopped them at different heights, which gives the tower its stepped outline. It is 442 m tall, with 110 storeys. More than 1.7 million visitors a year ride up to the Skydeck, the highest observation deck in the United States, where glass boxes jut out from the building.

buckingham-palace.name: Buckingham Palace
buckingham-palace.clue: A royal family waves from its balcony, and guards in tall bearskin hats change shift at the gates. It began as a duke's townhouse at the end of a long avenue.
buckingham-palace.blurb: It began in 1703 as a large townhouse for the Duke of Buckingham. George III bought it in 1761 for Queen Charlotte, and in the early 19th century John Nash and Edward Blore enlarged it with three wings around a courtyard. Queen Victoria was the first monarch to live here, from 1837, and a new east front with the famous balcony later closed off the courtyard. Today it is the monarch's official London home and office, and its forecourt hosts the Changing of the Guard.

one-world-trade-center.name: One World Trade Center
one-world-trade-center.clue: The tallest tower in its hemisphere reaches exactly 1,776 feet, after the year its nation declared independence, at the southern tip of a famous island.
one-world-trade-center.blurb: Designed by David Childs of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, it is the main building of the rebuilt World Trade Center in Lower Manhattan, and it opened in 2014. It takes its name from the North Tower of the original complex, destroyed in the attacks of 11 September 2001. Its spire reaches 1,776 feet (541 m), a number chosen for the year of American independence, making it the tallest building in the Western Hemisphere. Its square base turns into eight tall glass triangles as it rises, ending in a square turned 45 degrees.

windsor-castle.name: Windsor Castle
windsor-castle.clue: Monarchs have lived here for over 900 years, longer than in any other palace in Europe. Its round tower crowns a hill above the Thames, a short ride west of a great capital.
windsor-castle.blurb: William the Conqueror built the first castle here in the 11th century, soon after the Norman invasion, to guard the western approach to London. Monarchs have used it since Henry I, making it the longest-occupied palace in Europe. Inside the walls stands the 15th-century St George's Chapel, one of the masterpieces of English Gothic. The lavish state apartments were remodelled in the early 19th century for George IV. A fire in 1992 damaged more than 100 rooms, which were restored over the next five years.

al-masjid-al-haram.name: Great Mosque of Mecca
al-masjid-al-haram.architect: Unknown builders, enlarged by many rulers
al-masjid-al-haram.clue: The largest mosque on Earth surrounds a cube draped in black cloth, and millions of pilgrims walk around it each year, in a desert valley near the Red Sea.
al-masjid-al-haram.blurb: It is the holiest mosque in Islam and the largest in the world. At its centre stands the Kaaba, the cube draped in black cloth that Muslims everywhere face when they pray, and which tradition says Abraham built. The mosque has been enlarged many times by caliphs, sultans and kings, most dramatically in the 20th and 21st centuries. During the Hajj, millions of pilgrims walk around the Kaaba seven times. Its guardian is the King of Saudi Arabia, who carries the title Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques.

british-museum.name: British Museum
british-museum.architect: Robert Smirke; Great Court by Foster and Partners
british-museum.clue: A Greek-temple front of columns in a leafy literary district opens onto eight million objects, from the Rosetta Stone to mummies, around a courtyard roofed in a glass lattice.
british-museum.blurb: Founded in 1753 on the collection of the physician Sir Hans Sloane, it was the world's first public national museum, opening in 1759 in Montagu House. Robert Smirke's Greek Revival building replaced the old house in the 19th century, behind a grand row of Ionic columns. In 2000 Norman Foster covered its inner courtyard with a roof of glass and steel, creating the Great Court. Its collection of about eight million objects, the Rosetta Stone among them, is the largest of its kind. Many were acquired during the British Empire, which keeps debates about returning them alive.

metropolitan-museum-of-art.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art
metropolitan-museum-of-art.architect: Calvert Vaux, Richard Morris Hunt and others
metropolitan-museum-of-art.clue: A Beaux-Arts palace of art on the edge of a huge urban park, whose grand front steps fill with celebrities in outrageous outfits every May for a famous fashion gala.
metropolitan-museum-of-art.blurb: The largest art museum in the Americas, it holds well over a million works in 17 departments, from an Egyptian temple to modern painting. Its main building sits on Fifth Avenue at the eastern edge of Central Park. The first part, opened in 1880, is now hidden inside later wings, and Richard Morris Hunt designed the grand Beaux-Arts front on Fifth Avenue. More than five million people visited in 2025. Each May its steps host the Met Gala, one of the most photographed nights in fashion.

united-states-capitol.name: United States Capitol
united-states-capitol.architect: William Thornton; dome by Thomas U. Walter
united-states-capitol.clue: A white cast-iron dome tops the hall where a nation's lawmakers meet, at one end of a long grassy mall. The city's street numbers all count outward from here.
united-states-capitol.blurb: William Thornton's design won the competition in 1793, and Congress first met here in November 1800, after the capital moved from Philadelphia. British troops set it on fire in 1814, and it was restored within a few years. The famous dome is not stone but cast iron painted white, added by Thomas U. Walter in the 1850s and 1860s, and finished during the Civil War. The building is also the starting point for the city's street numbers and its four quadrants. It stands at the eastern end of the National Mall.

st-paul-s-cathedral.name: St Paul's Cathedral
st-paul-s-cathedral.clue: A great Baroque dome raised after a fire burned a city's old cathedral down. Whisper against the wall of the gallery inside and someone on the far side can hear you.
st-paul-s-cathedral.blurb: Old St Paul's was largely destroyed in the Great Fire of London in 1666, and Christopher Wren was given the job of rebuilding it. His English Baroque cathedral was finished in 1710 on Ludgate Hill, the highest point in the City of London. Its dome, inspired by St Peter's in Rome, is one of the largest in the world and ruled the skyline for centuries. Inside, the Whispering Gallery carries a quiet voice all the way round the dome. Wren himself is buried in the crypt.

rock-and-roll-hall-of-fame.name: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame
rock-and-roll-hall-of-fame.clue: A glass pyramid leaning against a white tower on a Great Lakes shore, designed by the architect of the Louvre's pyramid, honours the loudest music of the 20th century.
rock-and-roll-hall-of-fame.blurb: Atlantic Records founder Ahmet Ertegun set up the Hall of Fame foundation in 1983, and after a long search Cleveland was chosen as its home in 1986. The city had a good claim: the local DJ Alan Freed helped popularise the term 'rock and roll'. I. M. Pei designed the museum, a glass pyramid leaning against a tower on the shore of Lake Erie, and it opened in 1995. Inside, it tells the story of rock through guitars, stage costumes and handwritten lyrics. New members are inducted every year.

milan-cathedral.name: Milan Cathedral
milan-cathedral.clue: A forest of white marble spires and thousands of statues, begun in 1386 and only finished in 1965. Visitors stroll across its roof in a northern fashion capital.
milan-cathedral.blurb: Construction began in 1386, and the last details were only completed in 1965, almost six centuries later. It is the largest church in Italy, since the bigger St Peter's is in Vatican City. It is built of pinkish-white marble from Candoglia, once brought down to the city by canal. Its roof bristles with spires and thousands of statues, and visitors can walk across its terraces among the pinnacles. On the highest spire stands the Madonnina, a gilded statue of the Virgin Mary and a symbol of the city.

tokyo-skytree.name: Tokyo Skytree
tokyo-skytree.clue: The tallest tower in the world, a white steel lattice 634 m high, its base a triangle that turns into a circle as it rises over a vast Asian capital.
tokyo-skytree.blurb: Completed on 29 February 2012 and opened that May, it is 634 m tall, the tallest tower in the world and the third-tallest structure. The number was chosen on purpose: read in Japanese as 'mu-sa-shi', it recalls Musashi, the old name of the region. It was built because high-rises had begun to block signals from the older Tokyo Tower, and it is now the main broadcast site for the Kantō region. Its base is a triangle that becomes a circle as it rises. Two observation decks sit at 350 m and 450 m.

florence-cathedral.name: Florence Cathedral
florence-cathedral.architect: Arnolfo di Cambio; dome by Filippo Brunelleschi
florence-cathedral.clue: Green, pink and white marble outside, and a huge brick dome that nobody knew how to build, until a goldsmith worked it out. A Tuscan Renaissance puzzle in stone.
florence-cathedral.blurb: Begun in 1296 to a design by Arnolfo di Cambio, the cathedral waited decades for a dome nobody knew how to build. Filippo Brunelleschi, trained as a goldsmith, won the competition and completed it in 1436 without the usual wooden framework, using bricks laid in a herringbone pattern and two shells, one inside the other. It is still the largest brick dome in the world. The outside is faced in green, pink and white marble, and the west front was only finished in the 19th century. Giotto's bell tower and the Baptistery stand beside it.

reichstag.name: Reichstag
reichstag.architect: Paul Wallot; rebuilt by Norman Foster
reichstag.clue: Visitors climb a spiral ramp inside a glass dome and look straight down on the lawmakers below, in a 19th-century parliament beside a river in a once-divided capital.
reichstag.blurb: Paul Wallot's Neo-Renaissance building opened in 1894 for the parliament of the German Empire. A fire in 1933 gutted it and helped the Nazis tighten their grip on power, and the war left it a ruin. After reunification, Norman Foster rebuilt it for the Bundestag, which moved in in 1999. His glass dome has a mirrored cone in the middle that reflects daylight down into the chamber, and visitors walk up a spiral ramp above the politicians' heads. In 1995 the artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude wrapped the whole building in silver fabric.

winter-palace.name: Winter Palace
winter-palace.clue: A mint-green and white Baroque palace of 1,500 rooms on a wide northern river, home to the tsars and now part of one of the world's greatest art museums.
winter-palace.blurb: The present palace, the fourth on the site, was designed by Bartolomeo Rastrelli and largely finished in 1762. It was the official residence of the Russian emperors until 1917. It is said to contain 1,500 rooms, 1,945 windows and 117 staircases. After a fire in 1837 it was quickly rebuilt. The storming of the palace in 1917, retold in Soviet paintings and in Eisenstein's film October, became a symbol of the revolution. Today it is part of the State Hermitage Museum.

topkap-palace.name: Topkapı Palace
topkap-palace.clue: Sultans ran an empire from these courtyards for nearly 400 years, on a hilly point where the Golden Horn meets a strait between two continents.
topkap-palace.blurb: Sultan Mehmed II ordered it built in 1459, six years after conquering Constantinople. For almost four centuries it was the centre of Ottoman government and the main home of the sultans, until they moved to Dolmabahçe Palace in 1853. Rather than one huge building, it is a series of four courtyards with pavilions, kitchens, a treasury and the harem, where the sultan's family lived. Its name, meaning Cannon Gate, was only given in the 19th century. Today it is a museum full of relics, jewels and manuscripts.

red-fort.name: Red Fort
red-fort.clue: Red sandstone walls of a Mughal emperor's citadel, where the prime minister raises the national flag every Independence Day, in a huge capital on the Yamuna.
red-fort.blurb: Emperor Shah Jahan commissioned it in 1639 when he moved the Mughal capital from Agra to Delhi, and it was finished in 1648. Its design is attributed to Ustad Ahmad Lahori, who is also credited with the Taj Mahal. Inside the red sandstone walls stood marble palaces, audience halls and gardens, blending Persian and Indian styles. Nadir Shah's army plundered it in 1739, and after 1857 the British demolished many of its buildings. Every year on 15 August, the Prime Minister of India raises the flag here and speaks to the nation.

sultan-ahmed-mosque.name: Sultan Ahmed Mosque (Blue Mosque)
sultan-ahmed-mosque.clue: Six minarets and a cascade of domes, with thousands of blue tiles inside that gave it its nickname. It faces an older domed giant across a square where chariots once raced.
sultan-ahmed-mosque.blurb: Sultan Ahmed I built it between 1609 and 1617, beside the old Hippodrome and facing Hagia Sophia. Its architect, Sedefkâr Mehmed Ağa, was a pupil of the great Sinan. A central dome rests on four half-domes, and the interior is lined with thousands of Iznik tiles and painted flowers in mostly blue tones, which gave it its popular name. It is unusual for having six minarets. The complex also includes Ahmed's tomb and a madrasa, and it is still a working mosque.

abraj-al-bait.name: Makkah Royal Clock Tower
abraj-al-bait.clue: The largest timepiece dials ever made glow from a 600-metre tower in a desert city, looming over the courtyard that millions of pilgrims travel to each year.
abraj-al-bait.blurb: The central tower of this seven-tower hotel complex is about 601 m tall, one of the tallest buildings in the world, and Guinness lists it as the tallest clock tower. Its four clock faces are the largest ever built. The government built the complex to house pilgrims right next to the Great Mosque, with design led by the firm Dar Al-Handasah. It is among the most expensive buildings ever made. Building it meant demolishing an Ottoman-era fortress on the hill, which drew protests from Turkey.

shanghai-tower.name: Shanghai Tower
shanghai-tower.clue: A glass skyscraper twisting a third of a turn as it climbs 632 m, the tallest in its country, standing beside two famous neighbours on the riverbank of a huge port city.
shanghai-tower.blurb: Designed by Gensler, it stands 632 m tall in the Lujiazui financial district, next to the Jin Mao Tower and the Shanghai World Financial Center. It is the tallest building in China and the third-tallest in the world. The tower twists about 120 degrees as it rises, a shape that reduces the wind load on the building. Two glass skins wrap around it, with sky gardens in the space between. Its lifts were the fastest in the world until 2017, at 20.5 m per second.

jumeirah-burj-al-arab.name: Burj Al Arab
jumeirah-burj-al-arab.clue: A hotel shaped like a billowing sail on its own artificial island, with a helipad jutting out near the top, just off a beach on the Gulf.
jumeirah-burj-al-arab.blurb: Designed by Tom Wright of Atkins and opened in 1999, it is one of the tallest hotels in the world, although 39% of its height is empty space. It stands on an artificial island 280 m off Jumeirah Beach, joined to the shore by a private curving bridge. Its shape copies the sail of a dhow, a traditional Arab boat. Near the roof, 210 m up, a helipad has hosted a tennis match and a golf drive. It became the symbol of the city's boom.

schonbrunn-palace.name: Schönbrunn Palace
schonbrunn-palace.architect: Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach and Nicolò Pacassi
schonbrunn-palace.clue: A 1,441-room summer palace painted in its very own shade of yellow, home of an imperial dynasty, with the world's oldest zoo in its garden, on the edge of a waltzing capital.
schonbrunn-palace.blurb: Its name means 'beautiful spring', after an artesian well whose water was drunk by the court. The Habsburgs used it as their main summer residence, and its Baroque form largely dates from the 18th century, designed by Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach and later reworked by Nicolò Pacassi for Empress Maria Theresa. Its 1,441 rooms sit behind walls in a colour so typical it is called Schönbrunn yellow. The gardens hold the oldest zoo in the world still running, founded in 1752. It has drawn crowds of tourists since the 1950s.

mosque-cathedral-of-cordoba.name: Mosque–Cathedral of Córdoba
mosque-cathedral-of-cordoba.architect: Commissioned by Abd al-Rahman I; cathedral nave by Hernán Ruiz
mosque-cathedral-of-cordoba.clue: A forest of hundreds of columns under red-and-white striped arches, with a Renaissance cathedral built right into the middle of it, in a hot Andalusian city.
mosque-cathedral-of-cordoba.blurb: Abd al-Rahman I, founder of the Emirate of Córdoba, ordered the Great Mosque built in 785, and it was enlarged several times over the next two centuries. Its prayer hall is a forest of columns topped with double arches striped in red brick and white stone. After Christian forces took the city in 1236, it became a cathedral. In the 16th century a Renaissance nave was built right in the middle of the hall. Emperor Charles V is said to have regretted it, saying they had destroyed something unique to build something ordinary.

tokyo-tower.name: Tokyo Tower
tokyo-tower.clue: An orange-and-white lattice tower modelled on a famous Parisian one, and a little taller, glowing over a giant Asian capital at night.
tokyo-tower.blurb: Completed in 1958, the lattice tower was inspired by the Eiffel Tower and stands 332.9 m tall. It is painted white and international orange to meet air safety rules, and repainting it every five years takes about a year. It was the tallest tower in Japan until Tokyo Skytree took over in 2012, partly because new high-rises had begun to block its television signals. Visitors can go up to a main deck at 150 m and a top deck at about 250 m. At its foot, a five-storey building holds shops and restaurants.

castel-sant-angelo.name: Castel Sant'Angelo
castel-sant-angelo.clue: A Roman emperor's round tomb beside the Tiber, later a papal fortress joined to the Vatican by a raised escape passage, with a bronze angel on top.
castel-sant-angelo.blurb: Emperor Hadrian built this huge cylinder as a mausoleum for himself and his family, and it was finished around 139 AD. For a time it was the tallest building in Rome. The popes later turned it into a fortress and linked it to the Vatican by the Passetto, a raised, walled passage they could flee along in times of danger. Its name comes from a legend that the Archangel Michael appeared above it in 590 to end a plague. A bronze statue of the angel stands on top, and today it is a museum.

jeronimos-monastery.name: Jerónimos Monastery
jeronimos-monastery.architect: Diogo de Boitaca and João de Castilho
jeronimos-monastery.clue: Stone carved with ropes, sea creatures and armillary spheres, paid for with spice-trade riches, near where an explorer set sail for India from a wide Atlantic river mouth.
jeronimos-monastery.blurb: It was built from the early 1500s near the spot where Vasco da Gama set off on his first voyage to India, and paid for by a tax on the profits of the spice trade. It is the finest example of the Manueline style, a late Portuguese Gothic full of carved ropes, shells, plants and armillary spheres celebrating the age of exploration. Monks of the Order of Saint Jerome lived here until 1833. In 1880 da Gama's remains were moved here, along with those of the poet Luís de Camões. Several kings are buried here too.

york-minster.name: York Minster
york-minster.clue: Its great east window holds more medieval stained glass than any other in the land. A Gothic giant inside old Roman and medieval walls, in the north of England.
york-minster.blurb: A church has stood here since at least 627, but the Gothic building was raised between 1220 and 1472. It is the seat of the Archbishop of York, the second-highest office in the Church of England. Its Great East Window, glazed in the early 1400s, is the largest area of medieval stained glass in the country. The minster mixes several stages of Gothic, from the Early English transepts to the Perpendicular east end. In 1984 lightning set the south transept roof on fire, and the heat cracked the rose window.

prambanan-temple.name: Prambanan
prambanan-temple.architect: Unknown builders of the Mataram kingdom
prambanan-temple.clue: Sharp stone towers, the tallest 47 m high, honour a Hindu trinity on a mostly Muslim island, between a smoking volcano and an old royal city.
prambanan-temple.blurb: Built in the 9th century, it is the largest Hindu temple site in Indonesia and second only to Angkor Wat in Southeast Asia. It is dedicated to the Trimurti: Brahma the creator, Vishnu the preserver and Shiva the destroyer. The central Shiva temple rises 47 m, ringed by smaller shrines; the compound once held 240 temples. Carvings on its walls tell the Ramayana, which is also danced as a ballet on an open-air stage nearby. Earthquakes have damaged it several times, and restoration still goes on.

basilica-of-san-vitale.name: Basilica of San Vitale
basilica-of-san-vitale.clue: An eight-sided brick church whose plain outside hides glittering gold mosaics of a Byzantine emperor and empress, in a former imperial capital near the Adriatic.
basilica-of-san-vitale.blurb: Consecrated in 547, this sixth-century church is one of the best-preserved works of early Byzantine art. Its plain brick exterior gives no hint of the inside, which is planned around an octagon and covered in mosaics. The most famous show Emperor Justinian and Empress Theodora with their courts, shimmering in gold and green. Ravenna had been the capital of the Western Roman Empire and later a Byzantine stronghold in Italy. It is one of eight buildings in the city on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

bolshoi-theatre.name: Bolshoi Theatre
bolshoi-theatre.architect: Joseph Bové; rebuilt by Albert Cavos
bolshoi-theatre.clue: Eight white columns and Apollo driving a bronze chariot crown the front of a famous ballet house, home to more than 200 dancers, in a snowy capital.
bolshoi-theatre.blurb: The company dates from 1776, and the present building was designed by Joseph Bové and opened in 1825. After a fire in 1853 Albert Cavos rebuilt it, keeping the portico of eight columns crowned by Apollo driving a four-horse chariot. The Bolshoi Ballet is the largest ballet company in the world, with more than 200 dancers, and its name simply means 'big'. A six-year restoration finished in 2011 brought back the original acoustics and decoration. The building appears on the 100-rouble banknote.

todai-ji-temple.name: Tōdai-ji
todai-ji-temple.clue: One of the largest wooden buildings in the world shelters a giant bronze Buddha, while tame deer wander outside bowing for crackers, in an old capital.
todai-ji-temple.blurb: Emperor Shōmu founded it in the 8th century, and it opened in 752, modelled on the great temples of Tang China. Its Great Buddha Hall shelters a bronze Buddha about 15 m tall. The present hall dates from 1709 and is smaller than the original, yet it is still one of the largest wooden buildings in the world. By the late 19th century its heavy roof was close to collapse, and a restoration from 1904 to 1913 saved it. Outside, hundreds of sika deer roam freely and bow for crackers.

dolby-theatre.name: Dolby Theatre
dolby-theatre.clue: Every year the film world's best-known golden statuettes are handed out here, inside a shopping mall on a boulevard paved with stars, in a sunny Pacific city.
dolby-theatre.blurb: Opened in November 2001 as the Kodak Theatre, it was designed by David Rockwell specially to host the Academy Awards, which have been held here ever since. It sits inside the Ovation Hollywood shopping and entertainment complex on Hollywood Boulevard, next to the TCL Chinese Theatre with its famous footprints in cement. Kodak's name came off in 2012 after the company went bankrupt, and Dolby took over. Between Oscar nights it hosts concerts and shows.

palace-of-fontainebleau.name: Palace of Fontainebleau
palace-of-fontainebleau.clue: A royal hunting lodge in a great forest south of a capital, where a defeated emperor said goodbye to his guard at the foot of a horseshoe staircase.
palace-of-fontainebleau.blurb: For eight centuries French rulers, from Louis VII to Napoleon III, came here to hunt in the surrounding forest, about 55 km southeast of Paris. Francis I turned the medieval lodge into a Renaissance palace, bringing in Italian artists who founded what became known as the School of Fontainebleau. Napoleon loved it and called it 'the true home of kings'. In 1814, after his abdication, he said farewell to his Old Guard in the courtyard below the horseshoe-shaped staircase. It became a national museum in 1927.

stirling-castle.name: Stirling Castle
stirling-castle.clue: A royal castle on a cliff-ringed crag guarding the lowest crossing of a Scottish river, where a queen was crowned at nine months old.
stirling-castle.blurb: It sits on a crag of hard rock with cliffs on three sides, guarding what was until the 1890s the lowest crossing of the River Forth. Whoever held it controlled the way into the Highlands, so it was besieged many times. Most of the main buildings date from the 15th and 16th centuries, when it was a favourite home of the Stuart kings. Mary, Queen of Scots, was crowned in its chapel in 1543 at just nine months old. The battles of Stirling Bridge and Bannockburn were fought within sight of its walls.

lakhta-centre.name: Lakhta Centre
lakhta-centre.clue: Europe's tallest building, a twisting glass spire 462 m high shaped like a flame, on the shore of a Baltic gulf at the edge of a northern city of canals.
lakhta-centre.blurb: At 462 m it is the tallest building in Russia and in Europe, and the northernmost skyscraper in the world. Designed by RMJM for the energy company Gazprom, it was built from 2012 and topped out in 2018. Its five wings twist as they rise to a spire, a shape meant to recall a flame. It stands on the shore of the Gulf of Finland, far from the historic centre, after an earlier plan to build a tower closer in drew protests over the skyline. Its top floors hold a public observation deck.

palazzo-pitti.name: Palazzo Pitti
palazzo-pitti.architect: Attributed to Filippo Brunelleschi; built by Luca Fancelli
palazzo-pitti.clue: A banker built this rough-stone palace to outshine his rivals, and then his rivals bought it. It stands across a Tuscan river from an old bridge lined with jewellers' shops.
palazzo-pitti.blurb: The core of the palace was built from 1458 for Luca Pitti, an ambitious banker who wanted a home grander than the Medici's. The design is often attributed to Brunelleschi, with Luca Fancelli building it. In 1549 the Medici bought it themselves, and it became the main residence of the Grand Dukes of Tuscany. They laid out the Boboli Gardens behind it and filled it with treasures. Napoleon later used it as a base, and it was briefly a royal palace when Florence was the capital of Italy. Today it holds several museums.

pashupatinath-temple.name: Pashupatinath Temple
pashupatinath-temple.clue: A Shiva temple with a gilded double roof beside a sacred river where open-air cremations burn day and night, in a Himalayan valley.
pashupatinath-temple.blurb: Dedicated to Pashupati, a form of Shiva, it is one of the holiest Hindu sites in South Asia. The main temple, with its two-tiered gilded roof and silver doors, stands on the banks of the Bagmati River, and only Hindus may enter it. Around it a vast precinct of shrines, ashrams and images has grown up over the centuries. On stone platforms along the river, cremations take place in the open. It has been part of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage Site since 1979.

holyrood-palace.name: Palace of Holyroodhouse
holyrood-palace.clue: A royal palace at the bottom of a cobbled mile, facing a castle on a rock at the top, between a ruined abbey and an old volcano in a northern capital.
holyrood-palace.blurb: It is the monarch's official residence in Scotland, at the opposite end of the Royal Mile from Edinburgh Castle. It grew from the guest house of Holyrood Abbey, whose roofless ruins still stand beside it, and has been the main royal home in Scotland since the 16th century. Mary, Queen of Scots, lived here, and her secretary David Rizzio was murdered in her private rooms in 1566. Much of the palace was rebuilt in the 1670s for Charles II, to designs by Sir William Bruce. The King spends a week here each summer.

kailasa-temple-ellora.name: Kailasa Temple, Ellora
kailasa-temple-ellora.architect: Commissioned by the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I
kailasa-temple-ellora.clue: Not built up but carved downward out of a single basalt hillside: a whole multi-storey temple to Shiva in the dry basalt hills of the Deccan plateau.
kailasa-temple-ellora.blurb: This temple was not built from stones but carved out of the rock: workers cut down into a basalt hillside and removed a vast amount of stone to free a complete temple. It was made in the 8th century and is usually credited to the Rashtrakuta king Krishna I. The tower over the sanctuary rises 32.6 m above the courtyard. It is dedicated to Shiva and named after Mount Kailash, his home in the Himalayas. It is the largest of the 34 Hindu, Buddhist and Jain cave temples at Ellora.

palace-of-culture-and-science.name: Palace of Culture and Science
palace-of-culture-and-science.clue: A wedding-cake tower given by Stalin to a central European capital on the Vistula. Locals joked its viewing deck had the best view in town, because from there you can't see it.
palace-of-culture-and-science.blurb: Designed by the Soviet architect Lev Rudnev and finished in 1955, it was a gift from the Soviet Union, in the style of Moscow's 'Seven Sisters' skyscrapers. Rudnev mixed in details from Polish Renaissance buildings and American Art Deco. At 237 m it was one of the tallest buildings in the world when it opened, and it stayed the tallest in Poland until 2022. It holds theatres, cinemas, museums and offices. Many Poles disliked it as a symbol of Soviet rule, but it has become a landmark of the city.

paro-taktsang.name: Paro Taktsang (Tiger's Nest)
paro-taktsang.clue: White temples cling to a sheer cliff high above a Himalayan valley, where legend says a guru flew in on the back of a tigress to meditate in a cave.
paro-taktsang.blurb: The monastery was built in 1692 around a cave, clinging to a cliff high above the Paro valley. Legend says Guru Padmasambhava, who brought Vajrayana Buddhism to the region, flew here on the back of a tigress more than a thousand years ago and meditated in the cave. It is the best known of thirteen 'tiger's lair' caves linked to him. Reaching it takes a steep walk of a couple of hours. A fire in 1998 destroyed much of the main building, and it was carefully restored.

kunsthistorisches-museum.name: Kunsthistorisches Museum
kunsthistorisches-museum.architect: Gottfried Semper and Karl von Hasenauer
kunsthistorisches-museum.clue: An emperor built twin palaces, one for art and one for nature, facing each other across a square on a grand ring road. This one holds his dynasty's paintings under an eight-sided dome.
kunsthistorisches-museum.blurb: Emperor Franz Joseph opened it in 1891 to house the vast art collections of the Habsburgs. Gottfried Semper and Karl von Hasenauer designed it as one of a pair of matching museums on the Ringstrasse, facing the Natural History Museum across Maria-Theresien-Platz. An octagonal dome crowns the building, and the paintings above the grand staircase include work by a young Gustav Klimt. It is the largest art museum in Austria, famous for its paintings by Bruegel, Vermeer, Raphael and Velázquez.

mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral.name: Mexico City Metropolitan Cathedral
mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral.clue: Built on top of an Aztec sacred precinct beside a vast square, this huge cathedral has been sinking unevenly into the soft clay of a drained lake.
mexico-city-metropolitan-cathedral.blurb: Spanish builders began it in 1573 on top of the sacred precinct of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan, next to the remains of the Templo Mayor. It took until 1813 to finish, so it mixes Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque and Neoclassical styles. Claudio de Arciniega drew the first plans, inspired by cathedrals in Spain. It stands on the north side of the Zócalo, one of the largest city squares in the world. Because the city sits on soft clay from a former lake, the cathedral sinks unevenly, and major engineering work in the 1990s stabilised it.

landmark-81.name: Landmark 81
landmark-81.clue: Glass tubes of different heights bundled like bamboo stems rise 461 m beside a river in the biggest city of a long, narrow Southeast Asian country.
landmark-81.blurb: Completed in 2018, it is the tallest building in Vietnam at 461 m, with 81 storeys. The design by Atkins is said to be inspired by a bundle of bamboo stems, a traditional symbol of unity and strength, with glass tubes rising to different heights. It stands on the bank of the Saigon River next to Saigon Bridge, on the site of an old logistics base. The tower holds a hotel, flats, offices, shops and an observation deck near the top. It is the centrepiece of a large riverside development by Vinhomes.

vaduz-castle.name: Vaduz Castle
vaduz-castle.clue: A prince still lives in this medieval castle on a terrace above the Rhine, looking down on the capital of one of Europe's tiniest countries, tucked between two Alpine neighbours.
vaduz-castle.blurb: It is the palace and home of the Prince of Liechtenstein, perched high above the capital, which took its name from the castle. Its oldest parts are medieval, and it was largely restored in the early 20th century. Prince Franz Joseph II moved in for good in 1938, the first ruling prince to live in the country. The castle is not open to the public, but on the national holiday, 15 August, people are invited into the garden. It looks across the Rhine valley to Switzerland.

etchmiadzin-cathedral.name: Etchmiadzin Cathedral
etchmiadzin-cathedral.architect: Founded by Saint Gregory the Illuminator
etchmiadzin-cathedral.clue: Often called the oldest cathedral in the world, founded soon after a Caucasus kingdom became the first to adopt Christianity, within sight of a snowy biblical mountain.
etchmiadzin-cathedral.blurb: Tradition says Saint Gregory the Illuminator built the first church here between 301 and 303, after King Tiridates III made Armenia the first country to adopt Christianity as its state religion. It was built over a pagan temple, and it is often called the oldest cathedral in the world. The core of today's building dates from 483 or 484, after a Persian invasion badly damaged the church. It is the mother church of the Armenian Apostolic Church and the seat of its head, the Catholicos. Its cone-topped domes are typical of Armenian architecture.

art-institute-of-chicago.name: Art Institute of Chicago
art-institute-of-chicago.architect: Shepley, Rutan & Coolidge; Modern Wing by Renzo Piano
art-institute-of-chicago.clue: Two bronze lions guard the steps of this art museum by a great lake, where you can stand before American Gothic and a lonely late-night diner.
art-institute-of-chicago.blurb: Founded in 1879, it moved into its Beaux-Arts building in Grant Park in 1893, the year of the World's Columbian Exposition. Two bronze lions by Edward Kemeys guard the entrance on Michigan Avenue. Its collection of nearly 300,000 works includes Seurat's A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, Edward Hopper's Nighthawks and Grant Wood's American Gothic. In 2009 Renzo Piano added the light-filled Modern Wing. It is one of the oldest and largest art museums in the United States.

buda-castle.name: Buda Castle
buda-castle.clue: A green-domed royal palace on a hilltop, reached by a little funicular, above a great river that splits a central European capital in two.
buda-castle.blurb: Hungarian kings first built a castle on this hill in the 13th century. The Baroque palace that fills most of the site went up between 1749 and 1769 and was later greatly expanded by Miklós Ybl and Alajos Hauszmann. It was badly damaged in the Siege of Budapest in the Second World War and rebuilt in a simpler style under communist rule. Today it holds the Hungarian National Gallery, the Budapest History Museum and the National Széchényi Library. A funicular climbs up to it from the Danube.

basilica-of-santa-croce.name: Basilica of Santa Croce
basilica-of-santa-croce.clue: Michelangelo, Galileo and Machiavelli all lie in this Franciscan church, on a square where a Tuscan city still plays a brutal historic football match.
basilica-of-santa-croce.blurb: The main Franciscan church of Florence was begun in 1294, possibly to a design by Arnolfo di Cambio, and consecrated in 1442. It was built on marshland outside the old city walls. So many famous Italians are buried or remembered here, among them Michelangelo, Galileo, Machiavelli and Rossini, that it is called the Temple of the Italian Glories. Inside are frescoes by Giotto. Its marble front was only added in the 19th century. In the square outside, the city still plays its rough historic football, calcio storico.

875-north-michigan-avenue.name: John Hancock Center (875 North Michigan Avenue)
875-north-michigan-avenue.architect: Bruce Graham and Fazlur Khan (Skidmore, Owings & Merrill)
875-north-michigan-avenue.clue: Giant X-braces criss-cross the dark sides of this tapering 100-storey tower, where a viewing deck tilts visitors out over a busy avenue by a great lake.
875-north-michigan-avenue.blurb: Still widely known as the John Hancock Center, it was designed by Bruce Graham and engineer Fazlur Khan of Skidmore, Owings & Merrill and topped out in 1968. When finished it was the second-tallest building in the world, after the Empire State Building. Its huge diagonal X-braces are part of the structure: they turn the outside into a stiff tube and saved a great deal of steel. The 100-storey tower tapers as it rises and mixes offices, flats and restaurants. On the 94th floor, a ride called Tilt leans visitors out over Michigan Avenue.

lotte-world-tower.name: Lotte World Tower
lotte-world-tower.clue: A smooth white-glass cone 555 m tall, said to echo traditional ceramics and a calligraphy brush, rising beside a lake and a theme park in an East Asian capital.
lotte-world-tower.blurb: Opened in April 2017, it is 555 m tall with 123 floors, the tallest building in South Korea and among the tallest in the world. Kohn Pedersen Fox shaped it as a smooth, gently tapering cone, inspired by Korean ceramics and the curve of a calligraphy brush. A seam runs up its side, pointing towards the old city centre. Near the top, a glass-floored observatory looks over the city, and a 'Sky Bridge Tour' lets visitors walk across the roof itself. It stands beside the Lotte World theme park and Seokchon Lake.

cathedral-of-the-holy-cross-and-saint-eu.name: Barcelona Cathedral
cathedral-of-the-holy-cross-and-saint-eu.clue: Thirteen white geese live in the cloister of this Gothic cathedral, one for each year of a young martyr's life, in the old quarter of a Mediterranean port.
cathedral-of-the-holy-cross-and-saint-eu.blurb: Built mainly in the 14th century, it is the seat of the Archbishop of Barcelona and stands in the heart of the Gothic Quarter. Its cloister, finished in 1448, holds the Well of the Geese, where thirteen white geese are kept, said to stand for the age of Saint Eulalia when she was martyred. She is buried in the crypt. The ornate neo-Gothic front was only added in the late 19th century, over the plain exterior typical of Catalan churches. A lift takes visitors up to the roof.

notre-dame-d-amiens.name: Amiens Cathedral
notre-dame-d-amiens.clue: The roomiest Gothic cathedral in its country, built in about fifty years, its carved front once painted in bright colours, on a ridge above the Somme.
notre-dame-d-amiens.blurb: Built almost entirely between 1220 and about 1270, a short time for a Gothic cathedral, it has an unusual unity of style. Its first architect was Robert de Luzarches. By interior volume it is the largest cathedral in France, and its nave vault rises about 42 m. Its west front is covered in carved figures, and light shows now project the colours they were once painted in. It came through both world wars largely intact. It stands on a slight ridge above the River Somme, about 120 km north of Paris.

temple-of-kukulcan.name: El Castillo (Temple of Kukulcán)
temple-of-kukulcan.clue: A stepped pyramid with 365 steps, where at the equinoxes the afternoon sun draws a shadow serpent sliding down the stairs, in the flat jungle of a big peninsula.
temple-of-kukulcan.blurb: The great step pyramid dominates the centre of Chichén Itzá, a Maya city at its height around 900 to 1000 AD. It is dedicated to Kukulcán, the feathered serpent god. Each of its four sides has 91 steps, which together with the top platform make 365, one for each day of the year. At the spring and autumn equinoxes, the afternoon sun casts triangles of shadow down the northern stairway, like a snake sliding down to the carved serpent heads at the bottom. Inside it, archaeologists found an older pyramid.

dancing-house.name: Dancing House
dancing-house.clue: A glass tower pinched at the waist leans into a stone partner like two dancers, on a riverbank among the Baroque and Art Nouveau of a central European capital.
dancing-house.blurb: Designed by Vlado Milunić with Frank Gehry and finished in 1996, it stands on a riverside plot left empty since an American bombing raid hit it by mistake in 1945. Gehry first nicknamed it Ginger and Fred, after the dancers Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire: the stone tower is Fred, and the pinched glass one is Ginger leaning into him. Its curves caused controversy among the city's historic buildings. Václav Havel, who lived next door, backed the project. Today it holds offices, a hotel, a gallery and a rooftop restaurant.

museum-of-fine-arts-boston.name: Museum of Fine Arts, Boston
museum-of-fine-arts-boston.clue: A granite temple of art with murals by a famous portrait painter in its rotunda and one of the largest Japanese collections outside Japan, in an old harbour city of New England.
museum-of-fine-arts-boston.blurb: Founded in 1870 in Copley Square, the museum moved in 1909 to its present building on the Fenway, designed by Guy Lowell with a granite front and a central rotunda. It owns more than 500,000 works and one of the largest collections of Japanese art outside Japan. John Singer Sargent painted the murals of the rotunda and the grand staircase. I. M. Pei added the West Wing in 1981, and Foster and Partners built the glass-roofed Art of the Americas wing in 2010.

casa-mila.name: Casa Milà (La Pedrera)
casa-mila.clue: Its wavy, rough stone front made locals nickname it 'the stone quarry', and chimneys like helmeted warriors guard its roof, in a Mediterranean grid of cut-corner blocks.
casa-mila.blurb: It was the last private house designed by Antoni Gaudí, built between 1906 and 1912 for Pere Milà and his wife Roser Segimon. Its rippling stone front, with hardly a straight line, made locals call it La Pedrera, 'the stone quarry', and it was controversial at the time. The twisted iron balconies were designed by Josep Maria Jujol. The stone façade supports itself, so the floors inside are open and walls could go anywhere, and it even had an underground garage. On the roof, chimneys and air towers look like helmeted warriors.

heidelberg-castle.name: Heidelberg Castle
heidelberg-castle.clue: A red sandstone ruin, wrecked by lightning and by French armies, looming over the old university town in a wooded valley where the Neckar leaves the hills.
heidelberg-castle.blurb: The first castle here was built before 1214 and grew into a grand palace of the Electors Palatine, now among the most important Renaissance buildings north of the Alps. Lightning destroyed the upper castle in 1537, and French troops blew up much of it in wars at the end of the 17th century. Partly rebuilt, it was struck by lightning again in 1764 and left as a ruin. Romantic writers and painters then made the red sandstone ruin famous. In its cellar sits the Heidelberg Tun, one of the largest wine barrels in the world.

tomb-of-cyrus-the-great.name: Tomb of Cyrus the Great
tomb-of-cyrus-the-great.clue: A simple gabled stone room on six steps holds the founder of a vast ancient empire. Its base has shrugged off earthquakes for 2,500 years on a high plateau north of the Gulf.
tomb-of-cyrus-the-great.blurb: It stands in Pasargadae, the first capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great in the 6th century BC. The tomb is a small gabled chamber of pale limestone resting on six stepped tiers. It is said to be the oldest base-isolated building in the world: its foundation lets it shift rather than crack, and it has survived many earthquakes. Ancient writers say Alexander the Great visited it and ordered it repaired. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site as part of Pasargadae.

wartburg.name: Wartburg
wartburg.clue: Hiding here in disguise, a rebel monk translated the New Testament into his own people's language in about eleven weeks, in a castle on a forested crag in the green heart of central Europe.
wartburg.blurb: According to legend it was founded in 1067, and it stands on a precipice 410 m up above the town of Eisenach in Thuringia. Saint Elisabeth of Hungary lived here, and in 1521 and 1522 Martin Luther hid here as 'Junker Jörg', translating the New Testament into German. In 1817 students gathered here for the Wartburg Festival, calling for a united Germany. Its romantic 19th-century restoration inspired King Ludwig II when he planned Neuschwanstein. Much of the interior dates from that time, but large medieval parts survive.

museo-nacional-centro-de-arte-reina-sofi.name: Museo Reina Sofía
museo-nacional-centro-de-arte-reina-sofi.architect: Francesco Sabatini; extension by Jean Nouvel
museo-nacional-centro-de-arte-reina-sofi.clue: Glass lift towers climb the outside of an 18th-century hospital, where a huge grey canvas of a bombed town hangs, in a high, dry inland capital.
museo-nacional-centro-de-arte-reina-sofi.blurb: Spain's national museum of 20th-century art opened in 1992 in a former 18th-century general hospital designed by Francesco Sabatini. Glass lift towers were added to the outside, and in 2005 Jean Nouvel built an extension under a vast red roof. Its most famous work is Picasso's Guernica, painted in 1937 after the bombing of a Basque town in the Spanish Civil War. The collection is strong on Picasso, Dalí and Miró. With the Prado and the Thyssen it forms the city's 'Golden Triangle of Art'.

frauenkirche.name: Frauenkirche (Munich Cathedral)
frauenkirche.clue: Twin brick towers with rounded green caps set the height limit for a beer-loving city near the Alps, and a footprint by the door is said to be the devil's own.
frauenkirche.blurb: Built by Jörg von Halsbach from 1468 and consecrated in 1494, it is the cathedral of Munich and a symbol of the city. Its twin brick towers, about 99 m tall, wear rounded domes added in the 16th century. After a local vote in 2004, new buildings in the centre may not rise higher than them. Near the entrance, a dark footprint in the floor is said to have been left by the Devil, stamping in anger. It is the largest hall church in the world, and it was rebuilt after heavy damage in the Second World War.

conwy-castle.name: Conwy Castle
conwy-castle.clue: Eight massive round towers raised in just four years by a conquering king, joined to a walled town on a tidal estuary in a mountainous western land.
conwy-castle.blurb: Edward I built it between 1283 and 1287 during his conquest of Wales, with Master James of St George as architect. It was part of a project to create the walled town of Conwy, and castle and walls together cost about £15,000, a huge sum at the time. Its eight great towers still stand. The castle survived a siege in the winter of 1294 to 1295, sheltered Richard II in 1399 and held out for the king in the Civil War until 1646. It is part of a World Heritage Site with Edward's other castles in north Wales.

mauritshuis.name: Mauritshuis
mauritshuis.clue: A small square palace beside a pond, where a girl with a pearl earring gazes out among Golden Age masters, in a seat of government near the North Sea.
mauritshuis.blurb: Built for Count John Maurice of Nassau and finished in 1641, the house was designed by Jacob van Campen in a calm Dutch classical style. It stands beside the Hofvijver pond, next to the Binnenhof parliament buildings. Since 1822 it has housed the Royal Cabinet of Paintings, a small collection of about 850 works, mostly from the Dutch Golden Age. Highlights include Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring and View of Delft, Rembrandt's Anatomy Lesson of Dr Tulp and Fabritius's The Goldfinch.

peace-palace.name: Peace Palace
peace-palace.clue: A Scottish-born steel magnate paid for this neo-Renaissance courthouse, where nations settle quarrels by law, in a seat of government by the North Sea.
peace-palace.blurb: It opened on 28 August 1913 to house the Permanent Court of Arbitration, created by the Hague Convention of 1899 in the hope of ending war through law. Andrew Carnegie paid for it, and Louis Cordonnier won the design competition. Countries sent gifts for the interior, from marble to tapestries and a huge vase from the Tsar of Russia. Since 1946 it has also housed the International Court of Justice, the main court of the United Nations. The First World War broke out less than a year after it opened.

hermann-castle.name: Hermann Castle
hermann-castle.clue: A medieval fortress with a tall square tower stares across a narrow river at another castle on the far bank, at the very eastern edge of the European Union.
hermann-castle.blurb: The castle was founded around 1256, when this area belonged to the Danish crown, and its first full stone walls went up in the early 14th century. The Livonian branch of the Teutonic Order bought it in 1346. Its tall square keep, the Hermann Tower, is the symbol of the town. Across the Narva River stands the Russian fortress of Ivangorod, so two castles face each other across the border. Narva lies on the eastern edge of Estonia and of the European Union.

griffith-observatory.name: Griffith Observatory
griffith-observatory.architect: John C. Austin and Frederick M. Ashley
griffith-observatory.clue: Three copper domes on a dry hillside above a sprawling Pacific basin. More people have looked through its free telescope than through any other in the world.
griffith-observatory.blurb: Griffith J. Griffith gave the land and left money for it on condition that entry be free, as it has been since it opened in 1935. The Art Deco building on the slope of Mount Hollywood looks out over the city, the Hollywood Sign and the Pacific. More than 9 million people have looked through its 12-inch Zeiss refracting telescope, the most viewed telescope in the world. Inside are a planetarium and exhibits about space. It has appeared in many films, most famously Rebel Without a Cause.

q1-tower.name: Q1 Tower
q1-tower.clue: A slim residential tower of 322 m, its spire inspired by an Olympic torch, the tallest in its country, rising from a surf beach on a sunny eastern coast.
q1-tower.blurb: Opened in November 2005, it was the world's tallest residential building until 2011 and is still the tallest building in Australia, at 322.5 m. Its name is short for Queensland Number One. The design is said to draw on the Olympic torch, and its spire is lit at night. Near the top, an observation deck looks over the beaches of Surfers Paradise and the green hinterland. It was named one of Queensland's icons during the state's 150th birthday celebrations.

speyer-cathedral.name: Speyer Cathedral
speyer-cathedral.clue: The largest Romanesque church still standing, in red sandstone with four towers, where eight medieval emperors and kings lie in the crypt, beside the upper Rhine.
speyer-cathedral.blurb: Emperor Conrad II began it in 1030 as a show of imperial power, and the east end and the vaults were built between 1090 and 1103. It is the largest Romanesque church still standing in the world, built of red sandstone with four towers and two domes. Eight emperors and German kings are buried in its crypt, along with several of their wives. French troops burned the town in 1689 and badly damaged it, and it was restored in later centuries. It has been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 1981.

dome-of-the-rock.drop: HOLD: disputed location, needs owner decision

church-of-the-holy-sepulchre.drop: HOLD: disputed location, needs owner decision

ram-mandir.drop: politically charged (built on the site of the demolished Babri Masjid)

peterhof-palaces-and-complex.drop: a palace and park ensemble, not one building

kotoku-in-temple.drop: famous for its Great Buddha statue, not a building
